https://telex.hu/kulfold/2026/09/24/oros.text: Menü Kereső Oroszország is részt vesz a decemberi G20-csúcson Külföld Pupli Anna Sára Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom Oroszország biztosan részt vesz a decemberi G20-csúcson, amit Miamiban rendeznek meg, jelentette be csütörtökön Dmitrij Peszkov, az orosz elnök sajtótitkára a TASZSZ orosz állami hírügynökség szerint. Arról viszont, hogy Vlagyimir Putyin elfogadja-e Marco Rubio amerikai külügyminiszter meghívását , Peszkov szerint még nem döntöttek. „A kérdést alaposan át fogjuk vizsgálni, és csak ezután születik meg a megfelelő döntés” – jegyezte meg a Kreml szóvivője. „Mindenesetre Oroszország szándékában áll továbbra is részt venni a G20 munkájában és az ennek keretében megrendezett valamennyi fórumon.” Rubio szerdán azt mondta, a Trump-kormány reméli, hogy Putyin elfogadja a meghívást, ami a külügyminiszter szerint akár az alapját is képezheti egy szélesebb körű megállapodásnak. Szerinte a meghívással azért sincs gond, mert a nemzetközi kapcsolatokban az egymással egyet nem értő feleknek is szükséges találkozni és tárgyalni, különben lehetetlen lenne megoldani ezeket a vitákat. Peszkov egyébként szintén szerdán beszélt arról egy sajtótájékoztatón , hogy Putyin kész találkozni Trumppal, de akkor még nem volt szó a G20-as csúcsról. Stasys Eidrigevičius And Everywhere I See a Face Graphotography October 30, 2026–February 14, 2027 Add to Calendar Exhibition opening: October 30, 6pm, featuring the performance The Birth of a Painting by artist Stasys Eidrigevičius Add to Calendar Stasys Museum Respublikos st. 40 Panevezys LT-35173 Lithuania Hours: Tuesday –Saturday 11am–7pm Sunday 11am–5pm info@stasysmuseum.com stasysmuseum.com Facebook / Instagram Stasys Eidrigevičius and the faces that surround him The photographs in which artist Stasys Eidrigevičius captured his parents and loved ones during childhood awaken memories, evoke a sense of tradition, and inspire respect. His paintings, by contrast, often provoke laughter, creating a witty and at times subtly grotesque atmosphere. These seemingly contradictory modes of perception converge in the artistic genre Eidrigevičius has been developing in recent years: graphotography . Bringing together the traditionally distinct disciplines of photography and drawing within the digital realm, graphotography may be understood as a form of photographic image transformed through digital intervention. In Eidrigevičius’s work, it serves as yet another means of expressing a unique creative vision of the world around him. Eidrigevičius is constantly sketching. Today, his sketchbook has been replaced by a smartphone and tablet, through which he playfully and ironically reprogrammes the views that surround him. “I see a face everywhere,” the artist says. He follows paths shaped by both nature and humans, returns in memory to the countryside, plays with fragments of recollection, and dives deep into reflections on the relationship between past and present, the persistence and transformation of values, creative processes, and the junctions between generations. He mourns and laughs. Symbolically, such contrasting emotions emerge through a combination of traditional artistic methods and contemporary technologies. Photographs of architectural motifs that evoke historical memory, elements of the natural and urban landscape, and details of everyday life are later complemented by digital drawings. Within these spaces, Eidrigevičius inserts pairs of small eyes that have become a signature feature of his artistic language, while digitally drawn portrait or profile lines create new images. Japanese audiences were the first to recognise Eidrigevičius’s graphotographic works. More than a decade ago, the artist began collaborating with the renowned Japanese writer and art historian Motoko Nakagawa. Their partnership focused on books in which Nakagawa wrote the texts and Eidrigevičius created colourful, evocative, and highly original illustrations. In 2022, the artist began digitally drawing over photographs and sending the resulting images to Nakagawa. Their usual working method was reversed: the visual narrative emerged first, followed by texts written in response to the images. This collaboration has since resulted in five books published in Japanese. In their most recent publication, the authors explore the relationship between Eidrigevičius’s masks and the realities of the pandemic. Eidrigevičius’s graphotography brings together personal and collective experiences, creating a visual dialogue between tradition and innovation. Presented in Lithuania for the first time, these digitally transformed images – accompanied by essays inspired by real people, objects, and events – invite viewers to look more closely at the world around them, to reflect on it, and to embrace the act of creation. https://www.oann.com/newsroom/freedom-of.text: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio (C), alongside Poland’s Foreign Minister Radosaw Sikorski (L) and Burundi’s Foreign Minister Édouard Bizimana (R), speaks as he chairs the first plenary session during the G20 foreign ministers’ meeting in Atlanta, Georgia on October 30, 2026. (Photo by Erik S. Lesser / AFP via Getty Images) OAN Staff Addie Davis 10:02 AM – Sunday, November 1, 2026 The G20 Foreign Ministers’ Meeting wrapped up in Atlanta, Georgia, over the weekend, with United States Secretary of State Marco Rubio stating that freedom of navigation was a focal point for the assembly. Rubio specifically condemned the attacks on commercial shipping by Iran as well as hostilities from the Iranian-backed terrorist group, the Houthis. Since the advent of the U.S.-Iran conflict at the end of February, disruption to international energy routes have made global shockwaves, especially with the de facto closure of the Strait of Hormuz early in the conflict. Though U.S. officials have asserted that the transit of commercial vessels, which U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) reported have brought more than one and a half billion barrels of oil into the global market since summer, continues through the vital waterway with the assistance of American forces, the Iranian threat to shipping has led to volatility in the energy sector. “We now live in a world where the Iranian regime actively and openly targets commercial vessels for attack — not naval vessels; we’re not talking about naval vessels; we’re not talking about submarines,” Rubio stated at a press conference on Saturday . “We are talking about them saying, ‘Here’s a commercial vessel with cargo, oil, natural gas, and we are going to try to sink it.’” “They are openly attacking vessels as a tool of statecraft. That’s the world we live in, and I think Central Command and the United States has done a phenomenal job of protecting this shipping,” the secretary continued. Rubio also referenced the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, where hostilities between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia have escalated in recent months, and the “hostile coercion” seen in the South China Sea and the Strait of Taiwan. At the closing @G20org Foreign Ministers’ Meeting, I made clear to our partners that secure supply chains are essential for growth. Critical trade routes including the Strait of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandeb Strait must remain secure and open to commerce. And we must continue to… pic.twitter.com/8vhPGnG4NO — Secretary Marco Rubio (@SecRubio) October 31, 2026 According to a Saturday statement from the chair of the meeting, a position designated to the host country, the ministers specifically discussed the topics of energy security, supply chain resilience and geopolitical tensions, which included the Straits of Hormuz and the Bab el-Mandeb. Rubio noted that under the administration of President Donald Trump, the U.S. has pushed for “the G20 to get back to basics.” “But the core of this meeting and the core of what the president’s vision has been for G20 is to bring the G20, which is primarily an economic forum, back to its core principle and purpose, and that’s what we tried to address in the agenda we outlined today,” the secretary noted on Saturday. The G20 has 19 country participants , as well as two regional governing bodies — the African Union and the European Union — and Rubio recognized that the initial obstacle to reaching consensus was identifying the problems. “But I think the first step is at least some universal acknowledgment that freedom of navigation matters, that critical minerals matter, that supply chains matter, that food security matters, not just to the countries at the table but to countries around the world, and I do think we have that,” he told reporters. However, he explained that agreement on solutions was a different matter for the forum. “Of course, I wouldn’t pretend to you today that we are close to finding universally accepted solutions to these problems, but I do think that among the G20 represented here are countries that are working together to solve some of them, particularly in the realm of supply chains and critical minerals,” he said. On the sidelines of the weekend’s ministerial, Rubio also met with several foreign ministers, including engaging in discussions with the Quad – the U.S., Australia, India and Japan – to address “progress on ongoing Quad initiatives and reaffirm commitment to a free and open Indo-Pacific” The State Department noted that October’s meeting was meant to set the stage for the G20 Leaders’ Summit in December, which the U.S. president will host, with world leaders convening in Miami, Florida. In Atlanta, @SecRubio led @G20org countries back to their core mission: Drive economic growth and strengthen economic security. The United States will continue leading these efforts with our partners in December at the G20 Leaders’ Summit in Miami, concluding our G20 presidency… pic.twitter.com/1Zdbx7U7w4 — Department of State (@StateDept) November 1, 2026 CORRECTION – 3:45 PM: ‘Bab al-Mandab’ changed to ‘Bab el-Mandeb’ Stay informed! https://www.amnesty.org.au/how-a-letter-.text: 12 November 2026 In 2001, Witek Hebanowski was a member of a local Amnesty group in Warsaw when he met another young activist while organizing an event at a festival. Together they hatched a plan to spend 24 hours writing protest letters to governments around the world. This spontaneous action grew into Amnesty International’s Write for Rights campaign, a global force for change which over the years, has demanded an end to injustices faced by more than 200 individuals and groups. As Write for Rights turns 25 , Witek, 49, tells us how he became an activist, why letter-writing is as important as ever in this digital age, and describes some of the cases that deserve our attention today. ONE SIGNATURE: NINE TIMES THE IMPACT What inspired you to become an activist? My father was a painter and my mother was an English teacher, but both of them were involved in anti-communist activities in Poland in the 1980s. I remember one 60-year-old guy, who used to come for English lessons, but in fact, he was smuggling opposition newspapers and stuff that was illegal and for which you could get arrested if you were caught with them. My family, especially my mother, but also my father, helped with distributing this material. At an early age, they would also take me to demonstrations where I would see the police beating protesters. Even the end of communism in Poland was brutal, in the sense of total censorship and violence against protesters. Communism ended when I was 11 – I remember it well – and by the age of 18 I had witnessed the big transformation of Poland from an oppressive country to a free country. When did you first join a local Amnesty group? I was 18 when I joined the Amnesty International Warsaw group, fresh out of high school. It was an absolute discovery for me when I went to the Amnesty International Poland AGM, aged 19, for the first time – meeting people from other cities and with the same ethos, the same strong values. But more importantly, they were not dreamers, they were people of action – ‘doers’. “more importantly, they were not dreamers, they were people of action – ‘doers’” What sparked the 24-hour letter writing session? We had a brainstorming session – I remember using a blackboard where we wrote about 40 ideas on it, and from these 40 ideas, we came up with three basic rules. The first idea was to write letters based on Amnesty International cases – in the end, it was 30 plus cases altogether. Then we had a second rule, which was to do this to celebrate Human Rights Day, to celebrate the anniversary of the Human Rights Declaration. So, let’s do this over 24 hours, starting Saturday, that was 14 December at noon, and ending on Sunday noon. We tried to promote it as an extreme way of spending your Saturday night, you know, instead of going to some clubs, you would spend the time writing letters to 4, 5, 6 AM. And then the third decision was like, okay, count how many letters we had written and give feedback to each other. So, then I wrote a letter to Amnesty International Poland’s other local groups to say we at the Warsaw group were planning this action. Would they join? How did it grow from there? I think we got about 5,000 letters for Write for Rights in 2002. Then we got 20,000, then 40,000. In the first four or five years of the campaign, we got to 100,000 letters. One of the reasons why it worked was it inspired the movement. We got pictures from around the world of people writing letters, people in Niagara Falls in Canada, people in Zimbabwe, in Pakistan, all writing letters. How does it feel to see how Write for Rights has grown into a global campaign, now 25 years old, with hundreds of peoples’ lives being changed? I’ve come to understand from this experience that there is nothing that is impossible. We have no limits in what we can do. I never thought that from being in the basement of the Amnesty Warsaw group, operating without any funding, that I would see John Legend or Jeremy Irons recording a video about why they were taking part in this action. It was beyond my imagination at the time. Why is the letter so powerful? When authorities receive thousands of letters, it works. It makes a change, starting in their mailroom. It also gives power to people who are in prison. It gives power to their families. It gives people this kind of self-esteem, and a sense of dignity to know their case matters to other people who have made a bit of effort to write – because we don’t write letters by hand very often now. We have to understand there are people who need this effort from your side, more than anything. It gives them a reason to go on. “We have to understand there are people who need this effort from your side, more than anything. It gives them a reason to go on.” Success sometimes means someone gets moved to a better prison, or they get released. Or we stop the death penalty from going ahead. So, letter-writing is still effective, and we should also understand how meaningful it is for people on the other side, receiving letters. Are there any cases of injustice that you feel deserve more attention right now? Bahruz Samadov ’s case is especially personal to me. He recently cut himself during a court hearing, and Amnesty International has called for his immediate and unconditional release. Bahruz was part of One Caucasus , an arts and education festival and long-term programme we created in Georgia as a safe and inspiring space for young people from across the Caucasus. He joined us in 2015, when he was 19. As an Azerbaijani, he met and worked with young Armenians there, built friendships, and this became part of his path towards peace activism and dialogue. There is also a personal Amnesty connection. When we organized the first global Write for Rights action, Amnesty International Group 133 in Cambridge, Massachusetts – Rick Roth’s group – provided the first and, in practice, the only budget we had: just a few hundred dollars to help organize an action across around 40 countries. That story is an important reminder of how Write for Rights itself began. Years later, the same Rick Roth became a strong supporter of One Caucasus. He helped us financially, fundraised for the project, and Amnesty was visibly present there as well . So, for me there is a double responsibility here. Bahruz was part of the space we created – and now he is serving 15 years in prison on fabricated “high treason” charges connected to his peaceful activism and contacts with Armenians. We have to stand with him. I would ask people to read Bahruz Samadov’s story , print this campaign poster , take a picture with it and post it with #FreeBahruz and send it to inna@innaprzestrzen.pl with “Free Bahruz” in the subject line. © Private What would you say to someone who is thinking about joining Write for Rights this year? Do it. I think one of the deepest forms of happiness is to become part of a great idea that is actually changing the world for the better. Write for Rights gives you exactly that experience – little by little, person by person. “I think one of the deepest forms of happiness is to become part of a great idea that is actually changing the world for the better.” And when you write a letter, sign a petition or join an action, you may one day feel a little of that extraordinary moment when someone walks out of an unjust prison sentence and wins back their freedom. You were part of that. ONE SIGNATURE: NINE TIMES THE IMPACT Amnesty International is a global movement of more than 10 million people who take injustice personally. We are campaigning for a world where human rights are enjoyed by all – and we can only do it with your support. Act now or learn more about our human rights work.
